standard.title: Meaning and style through syntax
standard.description: analyse how meaning and style are achieved through syntax
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation summarise ideas in texts (AC9E9LA06). They have not yet analysed how meaning and style are achieved through syntax including nominalisations, clause combinations and noun group abstraction.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how meaning and style are achieved through syntax.

nodes.label: Nominalisation and the construction of events
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify nominalisation in texts and analyse how it affects the way events are constructed and what information is made explicit or implicit.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one nominalisation in a provided text and explain how it affects what information about the event is made explicit or hidden.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how nominalisation across a range of academic, journalistic or political texts constructs events, making some actors and causes explicit and others implicit.
wider: Compare how nominalisation is used in scientific texts versus political texts, analysing how each uses nominalisation to construct authority and objectivity
Examine how nominalisation in news reports can obscure agency and responsibility for events
Analyse how nominalisation functions in First Nations Australian legal or advocacy documents to establish formal register and conceptual authority
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (clause combinations) and Node 3 (noun group abstraction) both depend on students understanding how nominalisation packages information — without this, analysis of complex clause and noun group structures has no grounding in how syntactic choice constructs meaning.

response_modes.reason: Nominalisation’s effect on meaning is highly context-dependent — its function in political language (obscuring agents) differs from its function in science (creating technical vocabulary); students need contrasting contexts to see the range.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Nominalisation is a high-leverage grammatical concept across academic, scientific and political discourse — comparative analysis across these domains offers substantial analytic depth for advancing students.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one nominalisation in a text
Explains how the nominalisation affects what information about the event or agent is made explicit or hidden

nodes.label: Clause combinations and logical relations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how logical relations between ideas are built through combining independent and dependent clauses, identifying the type of logical relation expressed.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one clause combination in a provided text that expresses a logical relation (e.g. cause, concession, condition) and explain the relationship it establishes.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how clause combinations across a range of texts build different logical relations — cause, result, concession, condition — and explain how these shape meaning and style.
wider: Compare clause combination strategies in literary and academic texts, analysing how each uses dependent clauses to build different kinds of argument or narrative logic
Examine how clause combinations in historical documents construct cause-effect relationships that shape interpretation of events
Analyse how complex clause combinations in First Nations Australian political or legal texts establish sophisticated chains of reasoning
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to analyse noun group abstraction and generalisation — a move that draws on understanding how complex clause patterns package and condense ideas into nominal forms. Without clause combination analysis, Node 3 syntactic analysis lacks its prerequisite scaffolding.

response_modes.reason: Identifying the logical relation expressed by a clause combination (particularly concession and condition) requires explicit instruction in the reasoning structure — students tend to identify clauses but not the logical work they do.

success_criteria: Identifies a clause combination and names the logical relation it expresses (e.g. cause, concession, condition)
Explains how the clause combination contributes to the meaning or style of the text

nodes.label: Noun group abstraction and generalisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how abstraction in a noun group allows for generalisation of complex ideas and explain its effect on meaning and style in academic texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one abstract noun group in a provided text and explain how it allows the text to generalise a complex idea.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how noun group abstraction operates across academic and analytical texts, explaining how it enables generalisation and contributes to formal style.
wider: Compare how noun group abstraction differs between student-written and published academic texts, identifying where students struggle to achieve the generalisation that abstraction enables
Examine how abstract noun groups are used in philosophical or theoretical writing to construct conceptual frameworks
Analyse how abstraction functions differently in persuasive political texts compared with academic analysis

response_modes.reason: Noun group abstraction draws on both nominalisation (node 1) and clause combination patterns (node 2) — at this node students coordinate all syntactic tools to analyse how meaning and style are constructed holistically.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Abstract noun groups are foundational to academic writing across all disciplines — analysis of how they function in published academic, philosophical and political texts is rich and transferable.
success_criteria: Identifies an abstract noun group in an academic or analytical text
Explains how the noun group enables generalisation and contributes to formal style
